title: Phase 3: Authentication and authorization
description: Implement NextAuth v5 with Google OAuth for the React frontend and cookie-based session validation in ASP.NET Core. Enforce organization-scoped RBAC, policy-based route authorization, and resource-level ownership checks.

data.text: Authentication answers "who are you?" Authorization answers "what can you do?" In an enterprise expense platform, both questions are nuanced: a user may authenticate via Google but must be mapped to an internal Organization, Department, and set of Roles before the system can make authorization decisions.

We use NextAuth v5 on the API side (under /api/auth) with Google OAuth. The React app delegates entirely to NextAuth for the OAuth flow. After successful sign-in, NextAuth issues a session cookie; the React app also stores a JWT in memory for API calls.

data.caption: End-to-end authentication flow
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User (Browser)
    participant R as React App
    participant N as NextAuth v5 (/api/auth)
    participant G as Google OAuth
    participant A as ASP.NET Core API
    participant D as Database (Users)

    U->>R: Click Sign In
    R->>N: GET /api/auth/signin/google
    N->>G: Redirect to Google consent
    G->>U: Show Google login
    U->>G: Enter credentials
    G->>N: Redirect with auth code
    N->>G: Exchange code for tokens
    G->>N: Return tokens
    N->>D: Upsert user profile
    N->>R: Set session cookie + JWT
    R->>A: GET /api/expense-reports (Bearer JWT)
    A->>A: Validate JWT + load OrganizationId
    A->>D: Query scoped by OrganizationId
    D->>A: Return reports
    A->>R: 200 OK + JSON

data.title: Roles and permissions
items: **Employee**: submit own reports, view own history, upload receipts.
**Manager**: view team reports, approve or reject within approval chain.
**Finance**: view all reports in organization, mark as paid, export.
**Admin**: manage users, departments, policy rules, organization settings.

terms.definition: Permissions assigned to roles, and users assigned to roles. Simple to reason about, but coarse-grained for complex scenarios.
Access decisions based on attributes of the user, resource, and environment. More flexible than RBAC but harder to audit.
A statement about a user (e.g., role=Manager, org=acme-corp) carried in a JWT or session cookie.

data.title: Always scope by OrganizationId
data.text: In a multi-tenant system, never trust the client to supply an OrganizationId from the URL. Extract it from the authenticated user's claims or JWT payload. A user from org A must never see org B's data — even if they guess a valid GUID in the route.

data.title: C#: Custom authorization handler for ExpenseReport ownership
data.content: A policy requirement handler enforces that a user can only approve reports where they are the next approver in the chain.

data.title: TypeScript: NextAuth v5 route handler with Google OAuth
data.content: The route handler creates or updates the user profile on sign-in and issues a session with claims needed by the API.

data.title: React: SessionProvider and role-based navigation
data.content: Wrap the app in SessionProvider and derive navigation links from the user's role.

data.title: Security: never trust client-supplied roles
data.text: The React UI hides links based on role, but the backend must independently verify authorization on every request. A user can modify JavaScript in DevTools and submit any request. All endpoints must validate claims server-side.

items: AUTH_SECRET: 32-byte base64 random string for NextAuth JWT encryption. Store in environment.
Database credentials in connection strings; never commit .env.
Cookie settings: HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax in production.

items.text: NextAuth v5 Google OAuth configured with session strategy = 'jwt'.
ASP.NET Core API validates JWT issued by NextAuth on every protected endpoint.
OrganizationId is injected from JWT claims; no client-supplied orgId trusted.
Authorization handlers enforce CanApproveReport, CanManagePolicies, etc.
React app conditionally renders nav links and protects routes via role guards.
Integration test proves user from org A cannot access org B's reports.

data.title: Phase 3 summary
points: NextAuth v5 handles OAuth and issues signed JWTs.
Backend validates the JWT signature and extracts OrganizationId + role from claims.
Policy-based authorization (not just [Authorize]) handles resource-level checks.
Frontend navigation is cosmetic only — backend enforces all access rules.
data.takeaway: Authorization is a backend concern, not a UI concern. If you skip server-side checks now, you will pay for it in Phase 4 when you expose sensitive financial data.
